content.title: Designing Effective Policy And Regulatory Frameworks
content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition

content.text:
Effective energy policies are the backbone of a successful and just energy transition 💬️. They guide investment, shape behavior, ensure access, and balance the interests of people, government, and industry. But policies often fail, not because of bad intentions, but because they ignore political realities, lack clear goals, or are poorly designed.
This module explores how to design effective and context-sensitive energy policies and regulations by focusing on tools like Institutional and Context Analysis (ICA), Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA), and adaptive policymaking. It emphasizes the importance of aligning policies across sectors, anticipating future challenges through strategic foresight, and continuously refining regulations based on evidence, feedback, and evolving conditions.
Lesson 1 Overview

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: A: Tailor Policies to Context

content.text:
Effective sustainable energy policies must be inherently context-specific, meticulously tailored to the unique needs, resource endowments, and socio-economic realities of each country. A one-size-fits-all approach is demonstrably ineffective given the vast disparities in energy access, economic development, technological capacity, and available natural resources across nations, particularly between developed and developing countries. The principle of "common but differentiated responsibilities," enshrined in international agreements like the UNFCCC, explicitly acknowledges these varying capabilities and contributions to climate change, necessitating diverse approaches and levels of commitment.
Developing countries, in particular, benefit immensely from policies that reflect their specific circumstances. For instance, the UNFCCC Technology Executive Committee (TEC), UNIDO, and UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre have developed a guidebook specifically to support developing countries in identifying, prioritizing, and implementing renewable energy technologies based on their national circumstances and development priorities. This guidance emphasizes considering economic feasibility, mitigation potential, deployment barriers, climate resilience, and just transition aspects relevant to local contexts.

The term “institutional and context analysis” refers to analyses that focus on political and institutional factors, as well as processes concerning the use of national and international resources in a given setting and how these have an impact on the implementation of programs and policies.

In its simplest form, an ICA can be used to investigate why specific laws are not applied or policies not implemented in a given country in spite of any formal commitments and statements that may exist, and what realistically be can done about it.

ICA can be useful tool to understand the forces and specific factors of a country's cultural, social, gender and domestic political characteristics that can that can impact energy policy/projects outcomes, and to identify the actors that are likely to help or hinder a policy.

An ICA can be useful to support implementation of a particular reform, or a combination of them, by helping to identify the gaps between formal rules such as laws or regulations (or how things should work in theory) and informal ones (how things really work in practice), and to map those elements influencing the status quo. These could be political factors, cultural practices, or a general bias in the application of legislation favoring or neglecting one geographical region or ethnic group.’

ICA is conceptually grounded in a set of assumptions of how development works, from which we derive distinctive ICA questions that inform processes of institutional and context analysis. For each assumption there is a a set of distinctive questions that should be central to any ICA, as follows:

From a human rights-based perspective, ICA adds value to the formulation of development interventions.It helps to unpack the concept of political will and identify courses of action to address bottlenecks for claims holders - or change strategy, if the vested interests of duty bearers prove too powerful to challenge.

ICA is not a magic bullet with which to achieve better results, but it can help prevent failures and contribute to risk management.

In a climate of decreasing resources and increasing pressure to meet SDG goals, it is now more important than ever to ensure that investments in energy transition is well focused, with targeted interventions that are feasible and based on realistic expectations.
Assumption #1
Development requires a change in power relations and/or incentive systems.

Throughout human history, the levels of human and economic development seen today are unprecedented.

The widespread provision of public goods and the presence of democratic governance are historically rare. Nonetheless, socioeconomic and political systems have protected the privileges of the few according to the power they have. From this perspective, businesses, political parties, governments or ethnic groups can be expected to do what is best for the country only if it does not threaten their own privilege.
Guiding Questions

What past conditions have led to historic pro-development or pro-poor policies in the country, such as laws relating to universal primary schooling, the enfranchisement of women, or the loosening of restrictions on the media?

Did these advances occur following major social movements or a post-conflict settlement, as a result of major electoral changes, or for some other reason?
Assumption #2
The powerful reward their supporters before anyone else.

ICA focuses on the logic of political survival. Those in power must reward those who put them there before they can reward anyone else. Where governments are elected, the core constituents of the incumbent, such as those from a particular economic class or ethnic group, will likely be the beneficiaries of more responsive governance. Where governments are not elected, the core constituents may be military or religious authorities. They, too, will be the beneficiaries of the most responsive governance.
Guiding Questions

On whom do the powerful depend to keep them in power? How are supporters rewarded?
What is the ability of those out of power, and those they represent, to protect their rights and have their voices heard? What other fault lines exist among those out of power?
Assumption #3
All actors in society have interests and incentives.

Rather than assume that everyone in society wants development for everyone, ICA assumes that some actors face incentives that put their private and public interests against one another.

For example, businesses may benefit from a state that is wealthy enough to provide good roads, reliable electric grids, and effective contract enforcement. But businesses may also benefit if they can use political influence to keep competitors out of their markets. If successful, they may lower the competitiveness of their industry, thereby lowering aggregate economic growth, which in turn hurts the state's financial ability.

This means that broad groups, such as civil society, farmers and business owners, must be disaggregated. Power relations are omnipresent at every level of society, in communities, in businesses, in households and in families, and their impact on development efforts - both positive and negative - should be examined in detail.
Guiding Questions

1. Do not think in terms of political will. The term is vague and unhelpful. Ask instead, 'what are the political incentives?'

2. What incentives could make actors put public interest before private interest? Can these private interests be leveraged for public gain?
Assumption #4
Resources shape incentives

The source of public revenue shapes the incentives of power holders to be more responsive to some groups than others. Reliance on revenue from state-owned oil or official development assistance, for example, contrasts with a reliance on revenue from private exporters, or the taxes of individuals.

Making some state institutions function effectively, while leaving others under-resourced or using them as sources of patronage, also shapes political incentives.

When development practitioners introduce new sources of revenue, they may unintentionally negatively affect this complex mix of resources.

This analysis can be taken right down to the community and household level, if desirable, because the family and the community are institutions whose choices and incentives are similarly influenced by the availability and distribution of resources.
Guiding Questions

1. What are the primary sources of revenue for power holders in the energy sector, and how do these revenue streams influence their responsiveness to public demands and accountability pressures?
2. In what ways does the presence of the UNDP or similar development actors influence the dynamics between power holders and local communities or civil society actors advocating for change?
Assumption #5

But all stakeholders
in society have constraints

The mere presence of an incentive does not mean an ability to act on that incentive. Institutions - formal and informal - shape actors' ability to act on their incentives. Institutions are systems of rules that regulate behaviour by establishing norms, rewarding compliance, and punishing violations. Systems of rules like constitutions or trade treaties establish limits on behaviour. Not all rule systems are formally encoded as law. Informal institutions serve the same purpose and should not be seen as weak or irrelevant. Indeed, in many developing contexts, informal rules that relate to things like kinship or patronage politics can matter more than formal rules written into law. Whether informal or formalized through laws and policies, gender relations are also systems that shape and/or constrain behaviour of individuals as well as of institutions.

1. Are major actors constrained by formal rules, or do informal rules seem to matter more? For example, do traditional or religious authorities enjoy significant influence in state institutions? How do gender relations influence the choices that individuals and institutions make?

2. If a group or organization has an interest in an issue, is there evidence of their ability to act collectively? Do they have a history of effective activism?
The primary objective of adopting this strategy to achieve sustainable energy goals through a more comprehensive and integrated framework for energy planning and management.

content.title: Timing and timeframe
content.body:
Ensure that the timing of the analysis is synchronized with the intended application. Lack of follow-up on the findings of an analysis may be because the analysis was not aligned with the relevant strategic or programming processes. The analysis report can therefore be left aside and quickly become outdated, particularly in crisis-affected countries or countries undergoing transitions.
An ICA has no specific duration, but most analyses will require data collection on site ranging from 5 to 10 working days of full-time work. Costs will depend on whether the consultant(s) involved is/are hired locally or internationally, and whether travel is required.

content.title: Buy-in and ownership
content.body: Identify in advance the actors whose buy-in is essential in following up the analysis and ensure that they are involved in the process. In some cases, follow-up depends on key actors. If they have not been involved in the analysis, or even in the design or the planning process, they may not feel the ownership needed to ensure that its recommendations are carried forward.

content.title: Handling sensitive information
content.body: Have a clear strategy to deal with findings that may be politically sensitive for the government or other actors. Because ICA includes questions related to the distribution of power and resources, the findings of the analysis can be very sensitive. Given that potential, a designated official should oversee the process from start to finish, ensuring consistency and accountability. Additionally, national stakeholders should be provided with a clear explanation of the analysis's purpose, emphasizing its role in enhancing effectiveness and supporting the country’s policy priorities.

content.title: Output from an ICA
content.body: Define in advance what kind of output is expected. The output of an ICA can be a debrief, workshop or report – or a combination of these. Workshops may be more suitable than reports to ensure that stakeholder engagement strategies are communicated and task forces are formed to implement them. Because an ICA will typically produce sensitive information, it is up to the agency or agencies that commissioned the report to decide whether, and how, to share the findings, externally.

content.text: To prioritize the broader public interest, legal and regulatory frameworks should seek a delicate balance to address power asymmetries and serve the goals and interests of people, communities, government, and industry with complete transparency and impartiality. This transformation is imperative not only for intrinsic reasons like fairness, human rights, and social justice but also for instrumental reasons, such as securing public support, fostering buy-in, ensuring effectiveness, and promoting long-term sustainability.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: B: Ensure Coherence Across Policies and Sectors

content.text: In the following section, we discuss some key strategies to enhance policy coherence in <ai prompt="What is energy governance?">energy governance 💬️</ai>

Policy coherence refers to the systematic alignment and integration of policies across various sectors to achieve consistent and mutually reinforcing outcomes. It involves ensuring that policies in different areas, such as economic, social, environmental, and governance, work together harmoniously, minimizing conflicts and maximizing synergies.
This approach aims to prevent situations where a policy in one sector undermines the objectives of another, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness and efficiency of policy interventions.

A coherent energy transition cannot proceed without clear signals from the top. Strong political will, anchored in executive mandates, national visions, or legal commitments, is necessary to prioritize coherence across energy, economic, environmental, and social policies. This includes embedding sustainable energy goals into national development plans and budgetary frameworks, and ensuring coordination is not derailed by short-term political cycles

Energy intersects with land use, water, transport, industrial policy, health, and more. Coherence requires mainstreaming energy goals into cross-sectoral planning, such as through national energy and climate plans or sustainable development strategies. Integration mechanisms, like inter-ministerial committees, policy impact assessments, or shared targets, can help ensure policies do not work at cross-purposes.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: C: Adaptive and Anticipatory Policy

content.text:
Adaptive policy-making refers to a flexible approach where policies are continuously reviewed, refined, and adjusted based on feedback, data, and changing circumstances.
Unlike traditional static regulations that rely on one-time, ex ante assessments of potential benefits and risks, adaptive policies incorporate learning mechanisms that allow for adjustments based on emerging scientific, technological, and social developments. These policies aim to minimize regulatory errors, such as overregulating beneficial innovations or under-regulating harmful ones, by using structured, sequential decisions.
Adaptive policies and regulations are governance frameworks designed to remain effective and responsive in the face of uncertainty, complexity, and evolving conditions. Unlike static policies that follow a fixed set of rules, adaptive policies integrate mechanisms for continuous learning, feedback, and modification to ensure their relevance and effectiveness over time.
Traditional regulatory frameworks often impose rigid requirements. While such rigidity is essential in areas like safety, grid reliability, and environmental protection, it can also stifle innovation and slow the transition to a sustainable energy system.
One effective way to encourage innovation is through performance-based regulations. Instead of dictating the exact steps industries must follow, these regulations establish desired outcomes, such as reducing carbon emissions or improving energy efficiency 💬️. This gives companies the freedom to explore multiple pathways, promoting competition and the development of cutting-edge solutions.

Moreover, adaptive policymaking requires continuous monitoring of regulatory impacts and incorporating feedback loops to refine policies over time. By establishing real-time data collection and performance tracking, policymakers can identify gaps, unintended consequences, or emerging challenges that require adjustments.
Key stakeholders in these monitoring efforts typically include government agencies (e.g., regulatory bodies and ministries), independent oversight institutions, academic and research institutions, civil society organizations, and private sector actors, especially those directly affected by the policy. Local communities and end-users also play a critical role in providing on-the-ground feedback.
Two specific methods to enhance adaptability in policymaking include:

content.title: Dynamic Policy Adjustment
content.body: Implement systems to regularly assess policy outcomes and incorporate feedback loops that allow for timely modifications in response to new data or unforeseen challenges.

content.title: Scenario Analysis
content.body: Utilize predictive modeling and scenario planning to anticipate potential future developments and stress-test policies against various possible futures.

content.text: Some features of adaptive policies:

content.title: Flexibility and Adjustability
content.body: Policies are designed with built-in mechanisms that allow them to evolve based on new data, emerging risks, or changing circumstances.

content.title: Evidence-Based Decision-Making
content.body: Adaptive governance relies on continuous monitoring, assessment, and the integration of scientific and empirical evidence.

content.title: Stakeholder Involvement
content.body: Regular engagement with diverse stakeholders ensures inclusivity and enhances policy effectiveness by incorporating multiple perspectives.

content.title: Scenario Planning and Resilience
content.body: Policies account for multiple possible futures, allowing for rapid adjustments in response to crises or unforeseen challenges.

content.title: Iterative Learning Process
content.body: Adaptive policies often follow a trial-and-error approach, adjusting based on real-world implementation outcomes rather than adhering to rigid frameworks.

content.text:
In times of rapid change and uncertainty, responsible policy must take multiple future possibilities into account. Strategic foresight offers the means to do that.

Policies that assume a continuation of past trends and fail to account for recent or emerging changes can prove ineffective, inadequate, or even counterproductive. This is ever more relevant in the case of climate change and the sustainability issues that arise from it, including those related to the energy transition.

Climate impacts pose significant risks to energy infrastructure and reliability, especially in the context of developing regions, such as Sub-Saharan Africa. Extreme weather events, such as droughts and floods, disrupt hydropower generation and damage transmission and distribution networks, while rising temperatures can reduce the efficiency of thermal power plants and increase energy demand for cooling. Additionally, shifts in weather patterns may affect the viability and predictability of renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind.

The purpose of strategic foresight is to equip governments and societies with the capacity to explore and prepare for multiple plausible futures and associated opportunities and challenges, spurring new thinking and assessing that strategic plans and endeavours are future-ready.

Strategic foresight informs measures of anticipatory governance, that is, the systematic embedding and application of strategic foresight throughout the entire governance process, including policy analysis, engagement, and decision-making. In energy governance, it helps decision-makers address uncertainties in the rapidly evolving sector.
Practical applications include:

content.title: Risk Management
content.body: Foresight acknowledges that the future is uncertain and that policy decisions inherently involve risk. It helps in identifying potential risks and developing strategies to mitigate them.

content.title: Resource Allocation
content.body: By anticipating multiple possible futures, governments can make more informed decisions about allocating limited resources for energy infrastructure and technology development.

content.title: Policy Flexibility
content.body: Foresight encourages the development of adaptive policies that can respond to changing circumstances, which is crucial in the face of rapidly evolving energy technologies and geopolitical situations.

content.title: Stakeholder Engagement
content.body: The foresight process often involves multiple stakeholders, helping to create more inclusive and robust energy policies.

content.title: Technology Adoption
content.body: Foresight can help in assessing the potential impacts of new energy technologies, allowing for more strategic decisions about their adoption and integration.

content.text: Strategic foresight employs a variety of methodologies to help organizations anticipate and prepare for future changes.
1: Horizon Scanning

Horizon scanning is a systematic process of identifying early signs of potential developments that could affect energy governance. This involves continuously monitoring a wide range of sources to detect emerging trends, technologies, and issues. The goal is to capture weak signals, early indicators of significant change, that may not yet be widely recognized.

By analyzing these signals, organizations can anticipate possible opportunities and threats, allowing for proactive strategy development.

Horizon scanning serves as the foundation for other foresight activities, ensuring that decision-makers are informed about the evolving external environment.
2: Megatrends Analysis

Megatrends analysis focuses on examining large-scale, long-term forces that shape the future of sustainable energy across multiple domains, such as social, technological, economic, environmental, and political spheres.

These megatrends are often interconnected and have complex, multidimensional impacts. Examples include demographic shifts, climate change, technological advancements, and globalization. By understanding these overarching trends, organizations can identify the driving forces behind change and assess their potential implications. This analysis aids in strategic planning by highlighting areas where significant transformations are likely to occur and allows for the alignment of strategies and initiatives with anticipated future developments.
Scenario Planning

Scenario planning is a method used to explore and prepare for multiple plausible future scenarios in energy transition. It involves creating detailed narratives that describe different ways the future of energy transition might unfold, based on varying assumptions about key uncertainties and driving forces.

The process typically includes the following steps:

content.title: Identifying focal issues or decisions
content.body: Determine the specific strategic concerns or decisions that need to be addressed.

content.title: Assess key drivers and uncertainties
content.body: Analyze factors that influence the focal issues, distinguishing between predictable trends and critical uncertainties.

content.title: Develop scenario frameworks
content.body: Construct a set of diverse scenarios by combining different assumptions about how key uncertainties may resolve.

content.title: Creating narratives:
content.body: Develop coherent and plausible stories for each scenario, detailing how the future could evolve under each set of assumptions.

content.title: Analyzing implications:
content.body: Examine the potential impacts of each scenario on the organization and identify strategic options.

content.title: Monitoring indicators:
content.body: Establish signposts or indicators to track which scenario (or combination thereof) may be emerging over time.

content.text: Engaging in scenario planning helps anticipate potential future developments and develop adaptable strategies that remain effective in different circumstances. This approach strengthens resilience by ensuring preparedness for a variety of possible outcomes.
4: Visioning and Backcasting

Visioning and backcasting are complementary techniques used to define desired future outcomes and plan the steps necessary to achieve them.

Visioning
his process involves stakeholders collaboratively creating a shared and detailed image of a preferred future state. It encourages creative thinking and helps to align organizational goals with long-term aspirations.

Backcasting
Once a vision is established, backcasting works backward from the envisioned future to the present, identifying the actions, policies, and intermediate milestones required to reach the desired outcome. This method contrasts with traditional forecasting, which projects forward from current trends; instead, backcasting starts with the end goal and determines the necessary steps to achieve it.

content.title: Box: Grenada’s Power System Integrated Assessment

content.text:
As discussed earlier, scenario planning is a critical tool in energy governance, enabling policymakers to explore multiple possible futures and develop strategies that remain effective under varying conditions.
A practical example of this approach is Grenada’s Power System Integrated Assessment which provided insights into Grenada’s energy transition by evaluating investment scenarios for least-cost intermittent renewable energy integration and network resilience.
The project aimed to enhance Grenada’s low-carbon energy transition and support a green recovery post-COVID-19. The assessment focused on improving the resilience of Grenada’s power network and increasing the integration of cost-effective, intermittent renewable energy sources.

The findings revealed that, under specific investment scenarios, electricity tariffs could be reduced by approximately 30%, offering valuable insights for short-term decision-making.
The figure below shows the historical and forecasted annual percentage variation of Grenada electricity demand for different years and scenarios

Key deliverables of the project included:
• Electricity Demand Profile: A comprehensive analysis of current and projected electricity consumption patterns to inform future energy planning.

• Renewable Energy Potential Assessment: An evaluation of Grenada’s capacity to harness renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, to diversify its energy mix.

• Generation Plans and Cost Review: A critical examination of existing power generation strategies and associated costs, identifying opportunities for optimization and cost reduction.

content.title: Box: IRENA scenarios for the Energy Transition

content.text:
IRENA utilizes long-term energy scenarios to guide clean energy transition planning and investment strategies. These scenarios help explore the complexities and uncertainties associated with future energy systems.

The Global Long-Term Energy Scenarios Network (LTES Network), launched under the umbrella of the Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM), serves as a platform for national energy planning institutions to exchange best practices. It supports initiatives like the G20 agenda by enhancing capacity in Emerging and Developing Market Economies to link energy planning with financial strategies for the transition. The LTES Network brings institutional support to its benefit around three areas:

IRENA’s LTES program includes workshops, regional events, and thematic webinars. In 2024, the webinar series "Energy Planning Frameworks for Mobilizing Finance for the Energy Transition" aims to connect energy planners and financial institutions to de-risk investments and improve collaboration. The series address leveraging planning frameworks to enhance investment outcomes and project feasibility while aligning with the G20 Energy Transition Working Group priorities.

content.title: Box: IRENA World Energy Transitions Outlook 2024

content.text: The 2024 Outlook underscores the use of foresight scenarios as a tool to support energy governance by helping decision-makers anticipate future trends, navigate uncertainties, and identify priority actions to address gaps across energy sectors. These scenarios inform the report's focus on three foundational areas: planning infrastructure development, refining policies and regulations to guide investments and address socio-economic impacts, and aligning institutional capacities with the evolving demands of a renewable-oriented energy system.

The figure below illustrates the investment requirements for the energy transition under the 1.5ºC scenario for 2024–2030, highlighting the need to close the investment gap. By incorporating foresight into governance, the report offers a framework to better align the energy transition with climate objectives and the pursuit of net zero emissions by mid-century.

This figure shows the dramatic increase in investment needed to meet the 1.5°C climate target by 2030. In 2023, global energy investments totaled about $2.6 trillion, but to stay on track, annual investments must rise to around $6.7 trillion between 2024 and 2030. Most of this will need to go toward energy efficiency, renewable energy, electrification, and grid upgrades. The total investment required over this period is $47 trillion, highlighting the urgency of closing the investment gap and shifting away from fossil fuels.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: E: Ground Policy Decisions in Data and Evidence

content.text: Effective sustainable energy policy design hinges on grounding decisions in robust data and evidence. This principle mandates the systematic collection, analysis, and utilization of empirical information to inform policy choices, measure progress, and ensure accountability. Evidence-based policymaking is essential for developing effective and targeted policies, enabling governments to understand the precise impacts of their interventions and to make necessary adjustments.
What is an RIA

A Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) is an evidence-based tool designed to support public decision-making. It involves a systematic appraisal of how a proposed policy is likely to affect various stakeholders and outcomes. RIA can be applied to primary legislation or secondary (implementing) regulations, and is utilized by central government departments, independent regulators, regional governments, and local authorities. When combined with community-based and participatory forms of assessment, RIA embodies a “whole-of-government” and “whole-of-society” approach, encompassing different types of policies, sectors, and institutions, and facilitating societal participation in the policy process.

Implementing RIA in developing countries presents unique challenges and opportunities. The World Bank has developed toolkits tailored to these contexts, emphasizing the importance of adapting RIA methodologies to local institutional capacities and policy environments.
Key considerations include:

content.title: Capacity Building
content.body: Enhancing the analytical and technical skills of policymakers and regulatory agencies to conduct effective RIAs.

content.title: Stakeholder Engagement
content.body: Ensuring inclusive participation of diverse stakeholders, including marginalized groups, to capture a wide range of perspectives and impacts.

content.title: Contextual Adaptation
content.body: Modifying standard RIA processes to align with the specific legal, economic, and cultural contexts of developing countries.

content.text: Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) for energy efficient lighting standards in Antigua & Barbuda

In 2018, Antigua and Barbuda conducted a Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) to guide government decision-making on implementing energy-efficient lighting standards. The assessment employed a multi-criteria analysis and cost-effectiveness evaluation, incorporating input from an expert panel. The study recommended a phased approach: initiating with voluntary incentives such as product subsidies or exchange schemes, and gradually transitioning to mandatory obligations for energy-efficient lighting. It also advocated for a third-party conformity assessment, requiring certification from accredited entities before products could enter the market.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: B: Key Principles for Using Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)

content.text:
There are three key principles for using Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) to create better policies and regulations:
Proportionality, Knowledge Utilization And Integration.

content.title: Proportionality
content.body: Proportionality: The methods and depth of analysis of RIA should be commensurate with the importance of the proposal under discussion. Light analyses are sufficient for incremental policy changes, recognizing that RIA depends on scarce resources like time and qualified personnel. Simultaneously, RIA can build public sector capacity for data generation and evidence-informed policymaking, as well as foster robust consultation processes

content.title: Knowledge Utilization
content.body: RIA provides practical knowledge that can be used by different actors in the policy process to formulate the final policy choice, considering the breadth and depth of delivered appraisals. Furthermore, maintaining a database and evidence to monitor laws and regulations after they enter into force makes RIA a “living” planning document.

content.title: Integration
content.body: RIA is more effective when integrated with other policy instruments and institutional designs. Combining RIA with policy evaluation, risk management, freedom of information, general principles of transparency and access to information, and an overarching framework of procedures for appraising policy options creates better regulation. Effective governance requires political commitment, training, up-to-date guidance material, and oversight mechanisms.

content.text: Global Database for Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)

This database contains documents related to Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) issued by or for national governments, or publications studying RIA as it is applied by governments worldwide. The database makes no claim that country documents are in force or are being used by governments. The database has been developed by the World Bank Group's Governance Practice, within the framework of the DFID and USAID funded Good Regulatory Practices (PDF) program.

takeaways.title: Coherence is the foundation of effective energy governance. Adaptive policies ensure resilience by integrating flexibility, monitoring, and stakeholder input. They evolve with new data, economic shifts, and environmental challenges, keeping energy regulations effective.

Adaptive policymaking and foresight make policies future-ready. Flexibility and learning mechanisms help policies respond to change and uncertainty.Scenario planning and real-time feedback ensure relevance over time.

Context-specific policies are crucial for just and effective energy transitions. One-size-fits-all approaches fail to address local needs, capacities, and constraints.Tailoring policies to national realities ensures feasibility, equity, and impact.
